paragraphs: Referring expression comprehension asks a model to locate the person or object described in language. This paper focuses on people and argues that existing benchmarks provide too few examples and too little linguistic variety to thoroughly assess modern multimodal models. HC-RefLoCo addresses that gap with longer descriptions that combine multiple kinds of evidence about a person.

The benchmark contains 13,452 images, 24,129 instances, and 44,738 reviewed annotations. Descriptions average 93.2 words, with a vocabulary spanning 18,681 words. They cover appearance, actions, location, interactions with objects, celebrities, and text appearing in images. This breadth makes the task more demanding than matching a short phrase to a single obvious visual attribute.

The evaluation also separates several aspects of performance. It measures localization under different overlap requirements, accounts for the size of the person being located, and includes assessments organized by subject. Experiments with 24 models demonstrate the benchmark's potential to challenge contemporary systems. Its contribution is a richer testing resource for understanding how models connect detailed language with human-centered visual evidence.
neurips-2024-a-large-scale-human-centric.tldr: HC-RefLoCo tests whether multimodal models can locate people from long, detailed descriptions using a large and varied benchmark.

paragraphs: Detecting lights from vehicles, traffic signals, and streetlights matters for driving and night vision, but these targets create a distinctive recognition problem. They can be extremely small and look alike despite coming from different sources. The paper introduces the YouTube Driving Light Detection dataset, YDLD, to support systematic research on this comparatively underexplored task.

YDLD provides more images and bounding-box annotations for multiple light sources than existing light-detection datasets. The authors analyze its statistics and compare transfer learning from other detection benchmarks to support its generality. They also evaluate recent object detectors, finding that the small size and similar appearance of lights lead to low detection scores.

The proposed improvements target those difficulties directly. A lightness focal loss penalizes misclassified examples more strongly, while a spatial attention prior incorporates lighting information and broader scene context. The authors also incorporate the loss into semi-supervised detection, producing SS-FLD. They report consistent improvements in mean average precision across various recent detector types on YDLD. Together, the dataset and methods establish a shared evaluation setting and demonstrate useful changes to how detectors learn from difficult light examples.
neurips-2024-a-new-multi-source-light-de.tldr: The paper introduces a driving-light benchmark and lighting-aware learning methods that improve several detectors on its small, visually similar targets.

paragraphs: Recognizing human activities from sensors requires balancing prediction accuracy with the speed needed for applications such as fitness tracking and health monitoring. Lightweight networks often pursue speed by limiting their depth or the connections within each layer. The authors identify a weakness in these designs: the final classifier uses only the features produced by the last layer.

CALANet changes which information reaches that classifier. It aggregates features from every layer, giving the prediction stage access to representations that would otherwise be excluded from its direct input. The aim is to improve recognition while preserving the efficiency that makes lightweight models suitable for real-time use.

The paper proves that CALANet has the same theoretical computation cost as conventional networks. This is a claim about computational cost, rather than a reported measurement of speed on every possible device. Evaluations on seven public datasets show that CALANet outperforms existing methods and reaches state-of-the-art performance. The results support the idea that improving access to features already produced throughout a network can increase accuracy without raising its theoretical computation cost.
neurips-2024-calanet-cheap-all-layer-agg.tldr: CALANet improves sensor-based activity recognition by combining features from all layers while retaining conventional networks' theoretical computation cost.

paragraphs: Sharing a trained graph neural network can reveal sensitive information even when its training graph remains private. This paper studies attacks that infer properties of that graph, such as the average default rate in a transaction network. The privacy concern is about characteristics of the training data that a model may indirectly expose.

Existing attacks often train many shadow models to learn how model behavior relates to graph properties. That process is expensive. The proposed method trains only a small collection of models on graphs and then creates additional approximate shadow models. To make those approximations useful, it measures their diversity using edit distance and evaluates approximation error with a theoretically supported criterion. A selection mechanism retains models that combine variety with low error.

Across six real-world scenarios, the method reports average improvements of 2.7% in attack accuracy and 4.1% in ROC-AUC while running 6.5 times faster than the best baseline. These findings show that approximation can make this form of privacy-risk assessment both cheaper and more effective in the tested settings. They also reinforce that withholding raw graph data alone does not prevent property leakage through shared models.
neurips-2024-can-graph-neural-networks-e.tldr: Approximated shadow models make attacks that infer private graph properties from shared neural networks faster and more accurate in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to acquire new tasks without losing what it learned earlier. One source of forgetting is conflict between updates: a change that reduces the current task's loss can point against changes that would help previous tasks. This paper investigates that interference and hypothesizes that correlations between data representations play an important role.

The proposed global alignment method aims to establish suitable relationships between representations across tasks. It constructs each task's data representations as task-specific combinations of pretrained token representations shared by all tasks. This gives otherwise separate tasks a common foundation: their representation correlations are grounded in the relationships already present among the shared tokens. The authors explore different ways to learn these combinations.

The method achieves reported state-of-the-art continual-learning performance without replaying past experiences. It also produces strong class-incremental performance through task-incremental training. These findings support the usefulness of coordinating representation structure across tasks, while the proposed explanation linking correlations to interference remains a hypothesis in the abstract. The central contribution is a way to encourage cross-task alignment during individual task learning.
neurips-2024-continual-learning-with-glo.tldr: Global alignment builds task representations from shared pretrained tokens to reduce forgetting, achieving strong continual-learning results without experience replay.

paragraphs: Object tracking means following a specified target across successive video frames. This paper develops a diffusion-based formulation because diffusion models offer two useful capabilities: conditioning generation on information identifying the target, and modeling correspondences over time to reconstruct actual video frames. Together, these capabilities connect target identity with the way visual content changes.

The authors argue that conventional diffusion's extensive mapping into Gaussian noise is unnecessary for this tracking task. DINTR replaces that part of the process with an interpolation mechanism inspired by classical image processing. The approach retains the useful conditioning and temporal modeling aspects of diffusion while changing the route used to connect visual information.

The paper describes this interpolation process as more interpretable, stable, and faster for tracking. It evaluates DINTR on seven benchmarks using five representations of the indication specifying the target, reporting favorable performance across that range. The breadth of these evaluations supports the method's promise as a flexible tracking formulation. The main idea is to adapt diffusion mechanics to the structure of tracking instead of relying on a noise-based process designed around visual generation.
neurips-2024-dintr-tracking-via-diffusio.tldr: DINTR adapts diffusion to object tracking through an interpolation process intended to improve speed, stability, and interpretability.

paragraphs: Subspace learning seeks a lower-dimensional structure within high-dimensional data. This paper studies a single-layer generative adversarial network as a method for learning that structure. Its focus is the training dynamics: how the model's features develop and how their interactions influence the learning process.

Using a rigorous scaling-limit analysis, the authors examine a setting where features can develop together rather than being learned sequentially. They find that interactions among features can accelerate training and improve performance, particularly when initialization provides no useful prior information. Experiments on synthetic data, MNIST, and Olivetti Faces connect the analysis with observed behavior on concrete datasets.

The paper also compares GAN-based subspace learning with conventional approaches, both theoretically and empirically. In those comparisons, all methods recover the underlying subspace, but the GAN obtains a more informative basis for it. A basis describes the directions used to represent that same space, so this distinction concerns how the recovered structure is organized. The authors attribute the advantage to the GAN's ability to generate new samples, identifying a benefit beyond simply finding the subspace.
neurips-2024-exploring-the-precise-dynam.tldr: Analysis and experiments show how interacting features help a single-layer GAN learn a more informative basis for a data subspace.

paragraphs: A randomized trial can provide strong evidence about a decision policy among its participants, yet those participants may differ from the population where the policy will be used. This creates an external-validity problem: conclusions supported within the trial may not directly describe outcomes in the intended target population.

The paper uses additional information about the target population's observed characteristics to model which individuals enter the trial. That sampling model connects the trial participants with the broader population. Because the model can be miscalibrated, the proposed method evaluates policies while allowing a specified range of errors in that model.

The contribution is a nonparametric method that produces certified, valid policy evaluations even with finite samples. Its guarantee applies under the specified range of sampling-model miscalibrations; it does not require pretending that the fitted sampling model is exact. The authors illustrate the evaluations on simulated and real data. The result is a way to make trial-based conclusions about a different population while explicitly incorporating uncertainty about how trial participation was selected.
neurips-2024-externally-valid-policy-eva.tldr: The method certifies trial-based policy evaluations for a target population under a specified range of sampling-model errors, even with finite samples.

paragraphs: Federated learning allows participants to benefit from a jointly trained model, but it can also reward agents that contribute little or nothing. Mechanisms designed to discourage this free riding face another problem: participants can give the coordinating server false information to escape their obligations. This paper makes truthful reporting a central part of the incentive design.

The proposed mechanism, FACT, combines three elements. A penalty system eliminates free riding, a competitive environment creates incentives to report truthfully, and the benefit of a better model encourages participation. The last element matters because discouraging misconduct alone does not explain why an agent would join; FACT also offers better performance than training independently.

The authors position FACT as the first federated mechanism to combine these three properties. Their experiments show that it avoids free riding when agents provide untruthful information and reduces agent loss by more than a factor of four. The findings support addressing contribution and honesty together: a participation mechanism must account for what agents actually do and what they tell the server about it.
neurips-2024-fact-or-fiction-can-truthfu.tldr: FACT combines penalties, competition, and participation benefits to prevent federated free riding and encourage truthful reporting.

paragraphs: The paper studies sampling from a log-concave distribution restricted to a convex feasible region. The setup assumes a Lipschitz function defining the density, a region contained within a ball of radius R, a barrier function, and a warm starting distribution. The challenge is to generate samples efficiently while respecting the region's geometry.

The proposed framework uses spectral approximations to the barrier's Hessian, which describes its local curvature. This enables a generalized soft-threshold Dikin walk that works beyond the logarithmic barrier. For a polytope described by n hyperplanes, the Lee-Sidford barrier yields a mixing bound with principal dependence d squared plus d times L squared R squared, alongside a logarithmic warm-start and accuracy factor. Each step costs approximately n times d to the power omega minus one, suppressing additional logarithmic factors.

The authors also extend the framework to spectrahedra, feasible regions defined by semidefinite matrix inequalities. There, the main mixing dependence becomes nd plus d times L squared R squared. Both results improve the cited prior mixing bounds. Their significance is theoretical: a broader barrier-based framework reaches the target distribution in fewer bounded steps under the stated assumptions.
neurips-2024-log-concave-sampling-from-a.tldr: A generalized Dikin walk uses approximate barrier curvature to improve theoretical sampling bounds for polytopes and semidefinite feasible regions.

paragraphs: Neuro-symbolic AI combines neural networks with explicit logical reasoning. The authors argue that existing benchmarks often use simple, fixed rules and offer too little sustained reasoning among interacting agents. LogiCity addresses this gap with an abstract urban simulator whose agents follow customizable rules expressed in first-order logic.

The simulator describes urban situations through semantic and spatial concepts, such as whether an agent is an ambulance or whether two agents are close. Users combine these concepts into rules governing behavior. Because the rules operate on abstractions, they can be applied across cities with different agent compositions. Users can also configure the abstractions themselves, changing the complexity of the reasoning required.

LogiCity supplies two tasks: sequential decision-making over long horizons and visual reasoning over a single step. Evaluations show advantages for neuro-symbolic frameworks in abstract reasoning, while revealing difficulties with more complex abstractions, extended multi-agent interactions, and high-dimensional or imbalanced data. The simulator's contribution is therefore both a flexible environment and a way to expose where combining learning with logic remains challenging.
neurips-2024-logicity-advancing-neuro-sy.tldr: LogiCity uses customizable urban logic and interacting agents to test neuro-symbolic reasoning at different levels of complexity.

paragraphs: Isolated sign-language recognition identifies individual signs, represented by gloss labels. Because sign languages differ across regions, a dataset for one language does not fill every regional need. This paper introduces MM-WLAuslan to address the lack of a dedicated large-scale word-level recognition dataset for Australian Sign Language.

The dataset contains more than 282,000 sign videos covering 3,215 commonly used Auslan glosses performed by 73 signers. Recording takes place in a studio using three Kinect-V2 cameras and one RealSense camera. The four cameras simultaneously capture the signer from positions distributed around the front half of the body, providing multiple views and modalities of the recorded signs.

The authors benchmark state-of-the-art recognition methods under multi-view, cross-camera, and cross-view settings. These settings allow performance to be examined under different arrangements of the available camera evidence. Results indicate that the dataset remains challenging for the evaluated methods. The contribution is a substantial Auslan-specific resource that supports both recognition research and investigation of how camera viewpoint and modality affect the task. Its stated recording setting is controlled studio capture.
neurips-2024-mm-wlauslan-multi-view-mult.tldr: MM-WLAuslan provides over 282,000 multi-camera videos for recognizing 3,215 individual Auslan signs and evaluating viewpoint-related challenges.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning policy can perform poorly when deployed in an environment whose dynamics differ from its training environment. Offline domain calibration addresses this by adjusting a source simulator's physics parameters using a fixed collection of target-domain observations. This approach is useful when collecting extensive new interactions in the target environment is impractical.

Madoc formulates calibration around matching the target distribution of trajectories, using learned classifiers to construct a bandit reinforcement-learning objective. It then tackles the large parameter space by dividing calibration among cooperating agents. A variational autoencoder groups physics parameters according to their similar effects on dynamics, and each group becomes the responsibility of a distinct agent.

These agents coordinate their calibration policies so that multiple simulator parameters can be adjusted together. The authors evaluate Madoc on 21 offline locomotion tasks from D4RL and NeoRL. They report stronger performance than the compared offline model-based learning, offline calibration, and combined offline-and-online approaches. The findings support organizing simulator calibration around interacting parameter groups, allowing static target-domain data to guide coordinated changes in a large physics-parameter space.
neurips-2024-multi-agent-domain-calibrat.tldr: Madoc uses cooperating agents to calibrate groups of simulator parameters from offline target data, improving results across 21 locomotion tasks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning networks must keep adapting because their changing policies alter the observations and rewards encountered during training. Networks can lose this ability to learn, a problem called loss of plasticity. This paper examines how that failure relates to internal representations in Proximal Policy Optimization, or PPO.

Experiments on Atari and MuJoCo show that PPO experiences declining feature rank and reduced capacity to fit targets. Stronger changes in the learning environment aggravate these effects and can drive the actor's performance to collapse regardless of how well the critic performs. This distinction matters because the network choosing actions can fail even when the component evaluating them is performing well.

The authors also investigate why PPO's trust-region mechanism, intended to constrain policy changes, does not prevent this collapse. They find that deterioration of the representation and degradation of the trust region reinforce one another. Their proposed auxiliary loss, Proximal Feature Optimization, regularizes representation dynamics. Along with other interventions, it mitigates performance collapse in the experiments. The result connects policy-update stability with maintaining representations that remain capable of learning.
neurips-2024-no-representation-no-trust-.tldr: The paper links PPO's performance collapse to deteriorating representations and trust-region behavior, and introduces a feature-regularization loss that mitigates it.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a compact student model to imitate a larger teacher, aiming to retain useful capabilities at lower deployment cost. This paper explores a different way to improve the student: increase its parameterization during training while preserving its inference latency. The distinction separates the resources useful for learning from those needed when the trained model is used.

The method decomposes the student's parameter matrices into higher-dimensional tensors. The authors describe this decomposition as efficient and nearly lossless, and use it to over-parameterize the relatively small student. They also introduce a tensor constraint loss that aligns the student's high-dimensional tensors with those of the teacher, providing an additional way to guide knowledge transfer.

Experiments across computer vision and natural-language-processing distillation tasks show significant performance improvements. The central finding is that a compact student's training representation can be expanded to help it learn without increasing prediction latency. The contribution therefore concerns both model parameterization and the transfer objective: the tensor construction creates additional training capacity, while tensor alignment links that capacity to the teacher's information.
neurips-2024-over-parameterized-student-.tldr: Tensor decomposition expands a student's parameterization during distillation, improving performance without increasing inference latency.

paragraphs: This paper asks when a joint probability distribution can be understood as arising from a collection of independent causal mechanisms at the level of structure. It introduces qualitative mechanism independence, or QIM-compatibility, to express that relationship using directed hypergraphs, the qualitative structures underlying probabilistic dependency graphs.

When the structure is an ordinary qualitative Bayesian network, compatibility reduces to the appropriate conditional-independence requirements. This connects the new definition to a familiar interpretation of graphical models. The hypergraph formulation can express more, including functional dependencies. It therefore gives structural meaning to relationships that go beyond those captured by conditional independence alone.

The framework also addresses cyclic causal graphs. The authors show that demonstrating structural compatibility essentially requires constructing a causal model, giving the compatibility notion a direct causal interpretation. They further establish connections with information theory and use cyclic structures to clarify a longstanding conceptual issue in that field. The contribution is a mathematical language for reasoning about distributions, dependency structures, and causal mechanisms within a shared notion of compatibility.
neurips-2024-qualitative-mechanism-indep.tldr: QIM-compatibility gives directed hypergraphs a probabilistic and causal interpretation that includes conditional independence, functional dependencies, and cycles.

paragraphs: Testing language-model robustness requires finding prompts that expose failures, but a collection of nearly identical attacks provides limited coverage. Rainbow Teaming treats prompt generation as a quality-diversity problem: the search should discover prompts that are effective while also differing from one another. It uses a black-box, open-ended search to pursue both goals.

The main experiments target model safety, including evaluations of Llama 2 and Llama 3. The method uncovers hundreds of effective adversarial prompts and reports attack success above 90% across all tested models. The authors also find that generated prompts transfer well between models, showing that the discovered failures are not confined to the model originally targeted.

The paper uses the generated synthetic data to fine-tune models and reports substantial safety improvements without reducing general performance or helpfulness in its evaluations. Additional applications to question answering and cybersecurity explore the method's versatility. These findings suggest that diverse adversarial search can serve both as a testing tool and as a source of training material, while the broader prospect of open-ended self-improvement remains a potential application.
neurips-2024-rainbow-teaming-open-ended-.tldr: Rainbow Teaming searches for diverse, effective adversarial prompts and uses the resulting synthetic data to improve model safety in experiments.

paragraphs: The Gromov-Wasserstein distance extends optimal transport to matching objects across spaces that cannot be compared directly. Its underlying optimization problem is a nonconvex quadratic program, and existing solvers generally find only locally optimal solutions. A local optimum does not establish that the best possible matching has been found.

The paper proposes a semidefinite-programming relaxation of this problem. It connects the relaxation to a Lagrangian dual augmented with constraints relating the linear and quadratic terms of transportation plans. This produces a tractable, polynomial-time optimization procedure whose solution can, in some instances, recover a globally optimal plan for the original problem.

A key benefit in those instances is an accompanying certificate of global optimality. The method can therefore establish that the recovered plan is truly optimal, rather than simply returning a good candidate. Numerical experiments suggest that the relaxation frequently achieves this outcome. The qualification matters: the paper provides exact solutions and certificates for some instances, supported by encouraging experiments, rather than a universal polynomial-time solution to every Gromov-Wasserstein problem.
neurips-2024-semidefinite-relaxations-of.tldr: A semidefinite relaxation can recover and certify globally optimal Gromov-Wasserstein matchings in some instances, with frequent success in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Recovering camera locations and orientations from images requires reconciling geometric relationships across views. This paper studies that synchronization problem using a block tensor built from trifocal tensors, which describe relationships among triples of views. The target is recovery of camera poses up to a shared global transformation.

The authors derive an explicit Tucker factorization showing that, under appropriate scaling conditions, the block tensor has multilinear rank (6, 4, 4), regardless of the number of cameras. This reveals a compact structure within a potentially large collection of three-view relationships. They prove that the rank constraint supplies sufficient information for camera recovery when the data are noiseless.

The low-rank structure motivates an algorithm based on higher-order singular value decomposition. Comparisons with state-of-the-art global synchronization methods on real datasets demonstrate its potential to substantially improve location estimates. The theoretical recovery statement remains conditional on noiseless data and the stated scaling conditions. The empirical results suggest that using relationships among triples of views can improve synchronization beyond approaches organized around pairs.
neurips-2024-tensor-based-synchronizatio.tldr: A low-rank structure in three-view geometry enables noiseless camera-recovery guarantees and motivates an algorithm with promising real-data location estimates.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection must distinguish two different kinds of change. A model should recognize inputs with unfamiliar semantic content, while still classifying familiar content when its appearance is altered by changes such as noise. The paper finds that strong detection results in existing methods can come at the expense of this second ability.

The authors report that classification accuracy can collapse even under slight noise and develop a theoretical account of the resulting sensitivity-versus-robustness dilemma. Their proposed algorithm follows from this analysis. It separates the uncertainty-learning objective from a Bayesian perspective, aiming to resolve the conflict between detecting semantic novelty and generalizing under changes in input conditions.

Experiments on commonly used benchmarks show superior performance, with state-of-the-art detection achieved without sacrificing generalization in the reported evaluations. The contribution is therefore a joint treatment of two requirements that should both support trustworthiness. Its findings argue for evaluating whether a detector preserves useful classification under shifts, alongside how well it identifies unfamiliar semantic inputs. The empirical success supports the proposed decoupling as a way to improve both.
neurips-2024-the-best-of-both-worlds-on-.tldr: A Bayesian decoupling of uncertainty learning improves detection of unfamiliar inputs while preserving generalization under input shifts in benchmark evaluations.

paragraphs: Protein language models require decisions about model size, training-data volume, and learning objective. This paper studies how to balance those choices within a compute budget. Its investigation uses 939 million protein sequences and more than 300 trained models, spanning 3.5 million to 10.7 billion parameters and 5 to 200 billion unique training tokens.

The authors observe different problems when repeatedly training on the commonly used Uniref database: diminishing returns for causal language models and overfitting for masked language models. They add metagenomic sequences to increase diversity and address these effects. From the resulting experiments, they derive scaling laws tailored to protein data for both Transformer training objectives.

The study also identifies scaling behavior when transferring from causal to masked language modeling, interpreting the benefit through estimated effectively transferred tokens. Finally, it tests the scaling laws through downstream comparisons involving large versions of ESM-2 and PROGEN2 under equal or smaller pretraining budgets. These evaluations cover generation, structure, and function. The contribution is empirical guidance for allocating training compute across model capacity, data, and objectives rather than simply increasing model size.
neurips-2024-training-compute-optimal-pr.tldr: Large-scale experiments derive protein-model scaling laws that guide how to balance model size, diverse training data, and objectives within compute budgets.

paragraphs: Open-ended object detection asks a system to discover objects without being given a list of categories at inference time. VL-SAM addresses this task by combining a vision-language model's recognition capabilities with the Segment Anything Model's localization capabilities. The framework connects these existing models without additional training and also produces object segmentation masks.

The connection uses attention maps as an intermediate signal. First, a module aggregates attention across the vision-language model's heads and propagates it across layers using regularized attention flow. A second module repeatedly selects positive and negative points from the resulting maps. These points become prompts that guide SAM toward the corresponding objects.

On LVIS, the method surpasses the previous open-ended approach in object detection while additionally providing instance masks. It also performs favorably on CODA, which tests difficult object-detection cases, and can incorporate different vision-language models and SAM variants. The findings support attention as a practical bridge between recognition and segmentation. Here, training-free refers to the combination requiring no further training, while the framework draws on capabilities already present in its component models.
neurips-2024-training-free-open-ended-ob.tldr: VL-SAM turns vision-language attention into segmentation prompts to detect and segment objects without category lists or additional training.

paragraphs: A preference for simple features has been proposed as one explanation for shortcut learning, but examining that idea requires a way to measure feature complexity. This paper introduces a metric based on V-information that captures whether extracting a feature requires complex computational transformations. It applies the metric to 10,000 feature directions in a standard ImageNet-trained model's penultimate layer.

The analysis finds a spectrum of feature complexities within the model. Simpler features dominate earlier in training, while more complex ones appear gradually. The study also traces how these features move through the network: simpler features tend to pass through residual connections, bypassing parts of the visual processing hierarchy.

The authors then relate complexity to influence on the model's decisions. More complex features tend to be less important, while important features become accessible at earlier layers as training progresses. They describe this as a sedimentation process that gives later computation foundational elements to build upon. Together, these observations connect feature complexity with learning time, internal routing, and decision importance in the studied model, offering a more detailed account of feature reliance.
neurips-2024-understanding-visual-featur.tldr: A feature-complexity metric reveals how simpler and more complex visual features differ in learning time, network pathways, and influence on predictions.

paragraphs: Many interface-automation benchmarks focus on simple tasks expressible in one sentence. VideoGUI instead evaluates visually driven tasks drawn from instructional videos, including professional or unfamiliar software and complex activities such as video editing. The goal is to test assistants on procedures whose visual conditions carry essential information about what must be accomplished.

The benchmark divides performance into three levels. High-level planning requires reconstructing procedural subtasks from visual conditions without language descriptions. Middle-level planning converts screenshots and goals into precise narrated action sequences. Atomic execution tests the actual interface operations, including clicking, dragging, typing, and scrolling. Separate measures make it possible to identify the level at which an assistant struggles.

Evaluations show that even GPT-4o performs poorly on these visual interface tasks, with high-level planning especially difficult. This finding highlights a gap between executing an individual interface command and understanding a larger procedure from visual evidence. VideoGUI's contribution is a benchmark that exposes this distinction, providing more specific diagnostic signals than a single overall measure of whether a task was completed.
neurips-2024-videogui-a-benchmark-for-gu.tldr: VideoGUI separates visual interface automation into planning and execution levels, revealing substantial difficulties even for GPT-4o.

paragraphs: VisionLLM v2 brings visual understanding, perception, and generation into one multimodal framework. Its outputs extend beyond text answers to tasks such as object localization, pose estimation, image generation, and image editing. The aim is to support this variety through shared model parameters while allowing different user prompts to specify the desired task.

The central mechanism, called super link, connects the multimodal language model to task-specific decoders. It carries task information toward those decoders and passes gradient feedback back through the system during training. The authors report that it also resolves training conflicts among tasks, addressing a difficulty that arises when many objectives share one model.

To support the framework, the authors collect and organize training data from hundreds of public vision and vision-language tasks. This enables joint end-to-end training across the task collection. The resulting model achieves performance comparable to task-specific models while using shared parameters and different prompts. The contribution is a concrete architecture and training setup for combining many kinds of visual output within a generalist multimodal system.
neurips-2024-visionllm-v2-an-end-to-end-.tldr: VisionLLM v2 connects a shared multimodal model to specialized decoders, enabling joint training across hundreds of visual understanding and generation tasks.
